notes: THE NUMBERS ON THE SCREEN NOW MEAN WHAT THEY SAY. Behind this release is an audit that asked a different question from the usual one: not "is the entry right?" but "is what you are shown the same as what the ledger actually holds?" It found five places where they differed, in screens that six earlier audits had passed over. A DATED GENERAL LEDGER EXTRACT NOW OPENS WITH THE BALANCE BROUGHT FORWARD. Ask for one account from a date and the Balance column used to start at zero, which made it the movement for the period while still headed Balance. The gap against the cashbook was the opening balance, and it read exactly like an unexplained variance. The extract now carries a Balance brought forward line, computed over the same account, unit and project filters as the rows beneath it, on the screen, on the print and in the Excel export. A FOREIGN-CURRENCY BANK BALANCE IS STATED IN CEDIS, AND SAYS SO. The dashboard printed the cedi book value with the account's own currency code, so a dollar account holding ten thousand dollars read USD 125,000.00 — overstated twelvefold, on the first screen after sign-in. THE BUDGET METER MEASURES THIS YEAR'S EXPENDITURE BUDGET. It had divided spending by every budget line in the table, prior years and income budgets included, and could therefore report a comfortable position against a denominator matching no budget the organisation had approved. A BACK-DATED AGED LISTING CARRIES ITS CAVEAT INTO THE WORKBOOK — the artefact that gets filed and circulated as a year-end working paper — and the Entries column in the notes counts postings rather than date groups. THE ACCOUNT PICKER WORKS FROM THE KEYBOARD. Every account, vendor, bank, unit and project field shares one picker, and its rows sat in the keyboard's path but answered only to the mouse: you could tab onto an account, press Enter, and nothing happened. Type to search, arrow to the row, Enter to choose, Escape to close — and screen readers now announce it properly. Mouse behaviour is unchanged. IMPORTED SPREADSHEETS COME THROUGH ONE CHECKED DOOR. Bank statements and import sheets arrive from outside your organisation and are handed to a parser, so every workbook is now inspected on the way in and refused if it attempts to alter the running program. ALSO CARRYING THE PREVIOUS RELEASE, for which no notice was published: A REVERSAL ANNOUNCES ITSELF IN THE LEDGER, reading "Reversal of PV-…" rather than repeating the original's wording so that only the column told them apart. Reversals already posted keep their original wording — a ledger that edits its own history is not a ledger. The VAT return shows the GRA's decomposition of VAT, NHIL and the GETFund levy beneath the output figure, always adding back to the pesewa. And going live now requires a recovery code on file, alongside the registered name, an open period and automatic backups: for an offline ledger with no email reset, that code is the only way back in if the sole administrator forgets their password. Trials, testing mode and installations already live are unaffected. BEHIND THE RELEASE we also tested the upgrade nobody had tested — a ledger dozens of versions behind, brought forward in one startup against posted books, proving every voucher and every pesewa survives — and measured, for the first time, what this ledger feels like after five years of entries. THIS RELEASE CARRIES A DATABASE CHANGE. Your figures are untouched; please still back up first — Backup & Export, Back up now.
